content: The recent history of astronomy spans from approximately 1000 years before the present to today. The categorization of historical periods in astronomy is based on the understanding that modern astronomers, equipped with advanced training and technology, differ significantly from ancient observers. A key distinction lies in the use of technology, with the invention of the telescope being a major advancement for observational astronomy. The first practical telescopes, utilizing glass lenses, were developed in the Netherlands in the early 1600s (17th century). Astronomical history is typically divided into three main areas: archaeoastronomy, historical astronomy, and the history of astronomy. Archaeoastronomy, also spelled archeoastronomy, examines how ancient cultures understood celestial phenomena, how they utilized these phenomena, and the role the sky played in their societies. Clive Ruggles argues that it is misleading to equate archaeoastronomy with ancient astronomy, as modern astronomy is a scientific discipline, whereas archaeoastronomy focuses on the culturally symbolic interpretations of celestial events by different societies. Historical astronomy involves the scientific analysis of historical astronomical data. The American Astronomical Society (AAS), established in 1899, has a Historical Astronomy Division dedicated to fostering interest in the historical aspects of astronomy. This includes the history of astronomy, archaeoastronomy, and the application of historical records to contemporary astrophysical problems. Historical and ancient observations are used to study long-term theoretical trends, such as eclipse patterns and the motion of nebular clouds. Conversely, historical astronomers use computer models to validate ancient observations and to date historical records that might otherwise remain unknown. Astronomy is the oldest of the natural sciences, with origins in the religious, mythological, and astrological practices of prehistory. These influences are still evident in astrology, which was historically intertwined with public and governmental astronomy until their separation in the Western world a few centuries ago. In some cultures, astronomical data was used for astrological predictions. Ancient astronomers distinguished between stars, which remain relatively fixed over centuries, and planets, which exhibit noticeable movement over shorter periods. The constellation Andromeda is one of the 48 constellations cataloged by the 2nd-century Greco-Roman astronomer Ptolemy. Its depiction is rooted in Greek tradition. In Chinese astronomy, the stars of Andromeda were part of four different constellations with astrological and mythological significance. For example, nine stars from Andromeda, including Beta Andromedae, Mu Andromedae, and Nu Andromedae, along with seven stars from Pisces, formed an elliptical constellation called Legs. In Hindu mythology, a constellation related to Andromeda also exists. Earlier Babylonian astronomy depicted a female figure in Andromeda's location, representing a fertility goddess named Anunitum or the Lady of the Heavens. An Arab constellation called al-Hut (the fish) included stars from Andromeda, the Andromeda Galaxy (M31), and Pisces. Andromeda is also associated with the Mesopotamian creation myth of Tiamat, the goddess of chaos, whose body was used by Marduk to create the constellations as time markers for humans. In the Marshall Islands, Andromeda, Cassiopeia, Triangulum, and Aries form a constellation representing a porpoise, with Andromeda's bright stars forming the body, Cassiopeia the tail, and Aries the head. In the Tuamotu islands, Alpha Andromedae was called Takurua-e-te-tuki-hanga-ruki, meaning Star of the wearisome toil. The star Anser, officially named Alpha Vulpeculae, is the brightest star in the constellation Vulpecula. Located approximately 297 light-years from Earth, it forms a wide optical binary with 8 Vulpeculae. Anser is a red giant of spectral class M1, with an apparent magnitude of +4.4. It has been analyzed as a member of the Arcturus moving group, a collection of stars with high proper motion and metal-poor properties, believed to be remnants of a small galaxy consumed by the Milky Way. The constellation Antlia, representing an air pump, was introduced by Nicolas Louis de Lacaille in 1756 to symbolize experimental physics. Originally named la Machine Pneumatique, it was Latinized to Antlia Pneumatica in 1763. English astronomer Francis Baily later shortened the name to Antlia in 1845. The stars now comprising Antlia were once part of the ancient constellation Argo Navis, the ship of the Argonauts, which was divided into smaller constellations by Lacaille in 1763. However, due to the faintness of its stars, most authorities believe the ancient Greeks did not include Antlia in their depiction of Argo Navis. In Chinese astronomy, the constellation Dong’ou incorporated at least two stars of modern-day Antlia, including Iota Antliae, and was named after a place in Zhejiang province. Other stars in western Antlia, such as Epsilon, Eta, and Theta, were part of Tianmiao, the celestial temple, most of which lay in Pyxis. The faint southern constellation Apus was first defined in the late 16th century. It was one of twelve constellations created by Petrus Plancius based on observations by Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser and Frederick de Houtman. It first appeared on a celestial globe published in Amsterdam in 1597 or 1598 by Plancius and Jodocus Hondius. Plancius named the constellation Paradysvogel Apis Indica, with Paradysvogel being Dutch for bird of paradise and Apis Indica Latin for Indian Bee, though Apis (bee) is likely a mistake for Avis (bird).
